title: Molokoni
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Cow hoof stewed for hours in water with salt, onions and maybe a little tomato, until the meat is falling off the bones and the gristle has turned the liquid into a rich binding sauce.
longDesc: Molokoni is cow hoof soup, sold in kafunda joints across Kampala, and it is much-prized food that costs very little. It originates with both the Acholi of the north and the Itesot of the east, and it is known to many as nutritious comfort food. The ingredient list a vendor actually gives is short — water, salt, onions and maybe a bit of tomato — and the whole dish is hours of gentle stewing. The gelatinous gristle is what thickens it, and that is why it binds the way it does.
ingredients: Tomatoes — maybe a bit, per the vendor
// No quantities are documented in any Ugandan source
equipment: Large heavy pot, or a slow cooker
steps: Have the cow hoof sawn into pieces.
Put it in a large pot with water to cover, salt and the onions.
Add a little chopped tomato if you want it.
Bring it to the boil and then reduce to a gentle stew.
Stew for hours, topping up the water as it reduces.
It is done when the meat is very tender and falling off the bones, and the liquid has thickened into a rich binding sauce.
chefTips: Falling off the bones is the cue, and hours is the time. A crock pot or slow cooker overnight is the sensible modern route and the Ugandan sources say so themselves.
The gelatinous gristle is the thickener. Do not skim it off — it is what turns the water into a sauce and it is the whole character of the dish.
Keep topping the water up. Five hours of stewing will boil a pot dry and burnt hoof is unsalvageable.
Four ingredients is genuinely all a vendor uses: water, salt, onions and maybe a bit of tomatoes. Resist improving it.
One whole cow hoof yields five to six portions, which is worth knowing when you buy.

Some Ugandans believe it treats gout and joint pain. The author of the best Ugandan feature on it attributes the effect instead to the gelatinous gristle giving a rich binding sauce, which is an honest reading.

There is no quantified Ugandan molokoni recipe anywhere. The one Ugandan feature that prints quantities prints the Nigerian version, mokoto — a very different dish with dry sherry, Worcestershire sauce, dried ground shrimp and rice vinegar in it. I have not borrowed it and you should not mistake it for this.
Related dishes exist across the world and the Ugandan sources name them: Italian zampa buratta, Jewish petcha, Mexican beef soups.
commonMistakes: Cooking it for two hours and expecting it to be tender.
Using a Nigerian mokoto recipe and calling it molokoni.
sources: Adapted from 'Molokoni or cow's foot', Daily Monitor, 14 April 2012, Uganda at 50 series — which gives no ingredient list, no method and no quantities, and whose only preparation content is a vendor named Nalongo stating that she uses water, salt, onions and maybe a bit of tomatoes. Its principles are that the dish requires hours of gently stewing and should be cooked until very tender and falling off the bones.

Additional framing from 'Molokoni: Prized Ugandan dish', Daily Monitor, 1 September 2018: cow hoof stew as a much-prized dish relished by the hoi polloi, sold in kafunda joints across Kampala, with offal seen as an affordable alternative to beef, requiring extended cooking in a crock pot or slow cooker; a whole cow hoof yielding five to six portions; and the belief among some Ugandans that it treats gout and joint pain, which that author attributes instead to the gelatinous gristle producing a rich binding sauce.

That 2018 feature's only quantified recipe is the Nigerian variant, mokoto — three cow trotters, a kilo of offal, a kilo of goat, dry sherry, Worcestershire sauce, dried ground shrimp and rice vinegar among its ingredients. It is a different dish and is named here rather than used. There is no quantified Ugandan molokoni recipe in any source consulted.

That molokoni originates with both the Acholi of northern Uganda and the Itesot of eastern Uganda, is served in the majority of kafunda joints, and is known to many as nutritious comfort food, is from Sophia Musoki's Our Food Stories podcast, episode 14, with guest Sophia Aniku. That episode carries no method.
The Lugbara name putuku or mulokoni for cow leg is from the Wikipedia article on Lugbara cuisine.
storage: Refrigerate up to 4 days. It sets to a jelly when cold, which is a good sign.
healthBenefits: Long-stewed hoof gives collagen, glycine and proline.
High in protein with almost no carbohydrate.
Cooked in water with almost no added fat.
A cheap cut turned into a substantial meal, which is the point of it.
culturalNote: A kafunda is a small neighbourhood bar-restaurant, and molokoni is what it serves — cheap, slow-cooked, and eaten by people who work. That two communities at opposite ends of the country both claim it, and that it has close relatives in Italy, Mexico and Jewish cooking, says something true about what people everywhere do with a cow's foot.
